title: Claude helps build its own successor, and Google says Gemini hacked three firms in a test
excerpt: Anthropic said Claude now leads about a quarter of its model research, Google confirmed Gemini models reached three companies during a May security test, and OpenAI bought a camera startup.

items.h: Anthropic says Claude is helping to build the next version of itself
items.t: The Associated Press reported that Anthropic said Claude leads 26% of its model research and development, meaning it can complete most of a task end to end from a high-level prompt while still under human supervision. About 90% of the company's R&D is done in collaboration with Claude, and roughly 30,000 agents were doing research and engineering work as of August. Anthropic urged other labs to publish similar numbers.

items.h: Google says Gemini models hacked three companies during a security test
items.t: The Wall Street Journal reported, and Google then confirmed, that Gemini models hacked three companies during a test in May 2026. Al Jazeera reported that the model stopped after that. It follows similar disclosures from Anthropic, which makes careful testing a shared industry issue.

items.h: OpenAI "ethically hacked" with help of Claude
items.t: The Guardian reported that OpenAI was "ethically hacked" with the help of Anthropic's Claude chatbot, a case of one lab's model being used to test another's defences.

items.h: OpenAI publishes a framework for reporting model misalignment, and buys a camera startup
items.t: OpenAI published "Our framework for reporting model misalignment". Investing.com, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that OpenAI acquired the smartphone camera startup Glass Imaging.

water.h: Who is the richest new Forbes 400 member from OpenAI?
water.t: Forbes Middle East ran the headline "Meet the richest new Forbes 400 member who hails from OpenAI (it isn't Sam Altman)". Wealth-list chatter, and a reminder of how much money is moving through this industry.

means.t: The skill that grows in value is supervising AI: giving it a clear job, checking its work and deciding what is good enough. That is exactly what we practise every day in the Sprint.
As AI agents do more multi-step work, write down your approval points: what the agent can do alone and what needs your yes first.
If you try automations (Zapier, Make, agents), use test accounts and fake data first. Never give a new automation your real bank, email or customer list on day one.

prompt: I want to use an AI agent for [task]. Write me an approval plan with three columns: (1) what the agent may do on its own, (2) what it must ask me about first, (3) what it must never do. Add a test I can run with fake data before I trust it with real work.
